title: Composition
tagline: Planning, organising and drafting descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective pieces of writing.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Language (Paper 1) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus topic was taken from the official-verified ISC English registry entry; no CISCE examination paper was consulted, so every example and every practice question is original and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A good composition is not just a long piece of writing; it is a piece of writing with a clear purpose, a clear plan and a clear shape. In English Language Paper 1, composition means producing an extended piece of writing in a chosen form and register. This chapter looks at the four common types of composition asked in the syllabus — descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective — and shows how to plan, organise and revise each one so that the writing answers the question, stays on topic and uses language carefully.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Purpose and audience; descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective writing; planning; paragraphing; tone and register; revising and editing

learningOutcomes: Identify the purpose and audience of a composition.
Distinguish descriptive, narrative, argumentative and reflective writing.
Plan a composition before writing it.
Organise ideas into clear paragraphs with a beginning, a middle and an ending.
Choose tone and register appropriate to the task.
Revise and edit a composition for clarity and accuracy.

blocks.text: Before writing, decide what the task is asking you to do. A composition may ask you to describe a person, place or scene, to tell a story, to argue a point of view, or to reflect on an experience or idea. Each form needs a slightly different approach. Planning for a few minutes before writing usually improves the final piece more than rushing into the first sentence. A good plan states the main idea, the order of the points, and the kind of detail each paragraph will contain.

items: Begin by identifying the task, purpose and audience.
Descriptive writing should create an impression through sensory detail.
Narrative writing should have a sequence of events and some control of pace.
Argumentative writing should present a clear view and support it.
Reflective writing should show thought as well as experience.

items.text: If the task is to describe a crowded market, the plan might move from the general impression to sounds, smells and one or two striking details, rather than listing objects at random.
items.note: The plan decides the order; the order helps the reader follow the description.

blocks.text: Descriptive writing aims to bring a person, place, object or scene vividly before the reader. It relies on specific, concrete detail and on language that appeals to the senses. The best description is not a long list of everything visible; it selects the details that create the mood or impression the writer wants. Even in description, there is usually a point: the writer is describing this scene because it suggests something.

items: Use concrete, specific detail rather than vague general statements.
Move from the general to the particular, or organise the description in a clear order.
Select details that support the mood or impression.
Avoid overusing adjectives; precise nouns and verbs are often stronger.

items.text: Instead of saying 'the room was messy', a stronger description might mention clothes spread over a chair, books stacked unevenly, and a faint smell of dust. The point is not to pile on adjectives, but to give the reader something to see.
items.note: Good description is selective; it shows, rather than tells, what the scene is like.

blocks.text: Narrative writing tells a story, whether of a real event or an imagined one. A narrative needs a sequence of events, but it also needs more than one thing after another. There should be a clear beginning, a sense of change or development, and some control of pace. Short, quick sentences can speed up action; longer sentences can slow it down. Dialogue, if used, should sound natural and serve a purpose.

items: A narrative needs a clear sequence of events.
Show the order of events and how one leads to another.
Control pace with sentence length and detail.
Keep dialogue purposeful and believable in the context.

items.text: A short narrative about a missed train should not wander into unrelated detail; it should move from anticipation to the moment of discovery and then to the consequence.
items.note: The best short narratives have a shape, not just a beginning and an end.

blocks.text: Argumentative writing presents a point of view and supports it with reasons and examples. The argument should be clear and consistent, and it should deal with the question set rather than drifting into a general essay. A strong argument acknowledges the main counter-view and answers it, rather than pretending it does not exist. The conclusion should follow from the argument, not introduce a new point at the last minute.

items: State the main view clearly and early.
Support each point with a reason, example or illustration.
Consider the strongest objection to your view and respond to it.
Keep the conclusion in line with the argument.

items.text: If the topic is whether school uniforms should be compulsory, a good argument will not merely say 'they are good' or 'they are bad', but will give reasons and possibly weigh one side against another before reaching a conclusion.
items.note: The point is to argue, not just to assert.

blocks.text: Reflective writing looks back on an experience, idea or reading and explores what it meant or what it led to. It is personal, but it should still be organised and thoughtful. Reflection is not the same as a diary entry; the writer usually draws out a general insight from a specific experience. The best reflective pieces move from what happened to what it suggested or changed.

items: Make clear what is being reflected upon.
Move from the specific experience to a larger point.
Express genuine thought without becoming vague.
Keep the writing coherent, not just a collection of feelings.

items.text: A reflective piece on a school trip might begin with a particular moment on the trip, then move to what that moment suggested about teamwork, patience or observation.
items.note: Reflection works best when it is tied to a concrete experience and then developed into meaning.

keyPoints: A composition should have a clear purpose and audience.
Descriptive writing relies on specific, selective detail.
Narrative writing needs shape and control of pace.
Argumentative writing should support a view and address objections.
Reflective writing connects experience to thought.
Planning before writing usually improves the final piece.
Revision matters; do not stop at the first draft.
examFocus: Answer the exact task set, and make sure every paragraph relates to it.
A well-planned shorter composition is usually better than a longer one that drifts.

vocabulary.meaning: An extended piece of writing in response to a task.
Writing that creates an impression through detail and imagery.
Writing that tells a story or relates events.
Writing that presents a point of view and supports it with reasons.
Writing that explores the meaning or significance of an experience or idea.
The style and tone suitable for a particular audience and purpose.

questions.prompt: Descriptive writing is most likely to rely on:
questions.explanation: Descriptive writing is stronger when it uses precise, concrete detail rather than vague general statements.
questions.commonMistake: Piling on adjectives instead of choosing accurate nouns and verbs.

questions.prompt: In argumentative writing, a counter-argument is:
options: The opposing view that should be acknowledged and answered
questions.answer: The opposing view that should be acknowledged and answered
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the strongest objection makes the argument more convincing.
questions.commonMistake: Ignoring the other side instead of dealing with it.

questions.prompt: Give one reason for planning a composition before writing it.
questions.answer: Planning helps the writer keep to the point, decide the order of ideas, and avoid drifting into irrelevant detail.
questions.explanation: Planning is a way of organising the response before it is written.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking planning wastes time and that the best idea is to start immediately.

questions.prompt: What is one difference between narrative writing and reflective writing?
questions.answer: Narrative writing focuses on telling a sequence of events; reflective writing looks back on an experience and explores what it meant.
questions.explanation: Narrative writing is about the story; reflective writing is about the meaning drawn from it.
questions.commonMistake: Saying reflective writing is just a story with feelings added.

questions.prompt: Plan a descriptive composition entitled 'A Place at Dusk'. List the central impression, the main details you would include, and the order of paragraphs.
questions.answer: Central impression: a place that feels still and watchful as daylight fades. Paragraph 1: the general scene and the quality of the light. Paragraph 2: sounds and smells that appear in the evening. Paragraph 3: one or two particular details that give the place character. Paragraph 4: a closing image that repeats the mood. Each part should select details that support the impression.
questions.explanation: The plan should show the central impression and how the details work together to support it.
questions.commonMistake: Listing details without any unifying impression or order.
